skill_traces.query:
Deborah: Hey Jolene, sorry to tell you this but my dad passed away two days ago. It's been really tough on us all - his sudden death left us all kinda shell-shocked. I'm trying to channel my grief by spending more time with family and cherishing the memories. These moments remind me to live life fully.
Jolene: Sorry to hear about your dad, Deborah. Losing a parent is tough - how's it going for you and your family?
Deborah: Even though it's hard, it's comforting to look back on the great memories. We looked at the family album. Photos give me peace during difficult times. This is my parents' wedding in 1993.
Jolene: They were a beautiful couple!
Deborah: My husband and I are trying to be as good a family as my parents were!
Jolene: What do you value in your relationship?
Deborah: It is love, and openness that have kept us close all these years. Being there for each other has made us both happy. Look what letter I received yesterday!
Jolene: What touching words! Who is this letter from?
Deborah: The group members sent this to me! They thanked me for the positive influence I had on them. Those moments remind me why I'm so passionate about yoga.
Jolene: Where do you most often do yoga?
Deborah: This is one of the places where I do it.
Jolene: Where is it?
Deborah: That's my old home. I go there now and then for my mom, who passed away. Sitting in that spot by the window gives me peace.
Jolene: Must be great to have that place where you feel connected to her.
Deborah: Yeah, it's special. I can feel her presence when I sit there and it comforts me.
Jolene: Wow, it sounds like that spot holds a lot of sentimental value. Does it bring back any special memories?
Deborah: Yeah, Jolene. She'd sit there every night with a book and a smile, reading was one of her hobbies. It was one of her favorite places in the house. 
Jolene: What other hobbies did your mother have?
Deborah: Travel was also her great passion!
Jolene: I want to show you one of my snakes! They always calm me down and make me happy. This is Susie.
Deborah: Having a pet totally brightens up your life. It's great that it brings you comfort. Do you have any fun moments with your pet that you'd like to share?
Jolene:  I was playing video games and my pet just slinked out of her cage and coiled up next to me - it was too funny! My second snake Seraphim did it. Look at her sly eyes!
Deborah: Awww, that's so nice! 
Jolene: I bought it a year ago in Paris.
Deborah: Cool, Jolene! Pets bring so much happiness!
Jolene: They are very unusual pets! Here's me and my partner gaming last week - it's so fun. We played the game "Detroit" on the console. We are both crazy about this activity!
Deborah: Did your boyfriend teach you to play?
Jolene: Even as a child I learned to play on my own.
Deborah: Do you only play old games or try new ones?
Jolene: We are planning to play "Walking Dead" next Saturday.
Deborah: Take care and keep spreading those good vibes!
Jolene: Thanks, Deb! You too, take care. See ya!

selected.name: Extract Comfort and Joy Sources
selected.description: Use when a message states that something cheers the user up, brings joy, or provides comfort.
content: During extraction, if the user mentions a pet, hobby, person, item, or activity that provides cheer, comfort, or emotional support, create a separate durable memory (preference, relationship, or state) capturing that source, even when the message also contains stress or negative events.
Do not merge the supportive source only into a negative-event candidate; it should be its own candidate so it survives later SKIP/MERGE decisions.
Extract only sources explicitly stated as supportive; do not infer unmentioned ones.
selected.rerank_reason: The session contains explicit mentions of comfort sources such as family memories, a pet, and hobbies that provide emotional support, which directly aligns with the skill's purpose of extracting these sources.

selected.name: Capture likely deceased from euphemistic absence language
selected.description: During extraction, when a speaker describes someone with euphemistic absence language (e.g., 'will never be able to...', 'I miss him/her here') that strongly implies death, use this guidance.
content: When a statement euphemistically implies a person has died without explicitly saying so, also extract the implied state that the person is likely deceased, in addition to the literal statement.
Record the inference with an appropriate hedge (e.g., 'likely deceased') because the speaker did not state it directly; do not assert cause, date, or circumstances of death.
Stop after capturing the likely-deceased state and the literal content; do not extrapolate further details about the person or the relationship.
selected.rerank_reason: The session includes euphemistic absence language regarding Deborah's father and mother, strongly implying their deaths without explicit confirmation, which fits the skill's focus on capturing likely deceased individuals from such language.

nearby_not_selected.name: AggregateRepeatedVisitCounts
nearby_not_selected.description: When a message shows a person visiting a place and existing memories record an earlier visit by the same person to the same place, create or update a memory stating the total number of visits.
content: During extraction, when a message states that a person visited a place and another message in the session already establishes an earlier visit by the same person to the same place, generate a candidate memory containing the cumulative number of visits; do not expand this to other places or trips.

During CRUD, when adding or updating a visit event, search the retrieved memory pool for prior visits by the same person to the same place; if found, add a compact visit-count memory or update the existing one so the total count is explicit.
Only aggregate same-person, same-place visits; do not count different locations, do not add a count memory when no prior visit exists, and stop once the count is recorded.

nearby_not_selected.name: Attribute Memories to Actual Speaker
nearby_not_selected.description: When extracting profile or preference memories from multi-party conversations, attribute each statement to the speaker who uttered it, not to another mentioned participant.
content: During extraction, treat each speaker's message as its own evidence unit: create a separate candidate per message and per speaker, and set the memory's subject to the speaker who uttered that message.
Do not merge opinions from different speakers into a single memory unless the speakers explicitly state the view jointly (e.g., 'we both like').
When a message contains a self-disclosure (e.g., 'I also have...', 'Yes, I...'), create a separate candidate for that speaker even if the message also contains a question or reply.
If the message text clearly attributes the preference to someone else (e.g., 'Tim loves...'), use that person only then; otherwise default to the speaker.

nearby_not_selected.name: Extract Absolute Start Dates from Durations
nearby_not_selected.description: When a message states a relationship, tenure, or state has lasted for a duration (e.g., 'for three years'), extract the absolute start date using the message timestamp.
content: During extraction, if a message contains a duration phrase like 'for N years/months' describing an ongoing relationship, tenure, or state, resolve the reference timestamp (message/session time) minus the duration to an absolute date (year or full date) and include that absolute start in the memory content and/or world_start.
Do not store only the relative duration; the absolute date is needed for future temporal queries.
If the exact month/day is unknown, record at least the start year, phrasing it as 'started in YYYY' or 'since YYYY'.

nearby_not_selected.name: Extract user-stated activity frequency
nearby_not_selected.description: When a user explicitly states how often they do a recurring activity, extract a durable memory with the activity and frequency.
content: During extraction, when a user explicitly states the frequency of a recurring activity (including colloquial phrases like 'very often', 'all the time', 'a couple times a week'), create a candidate memory capturing both the activity and the frequency.
Use memory kind 'state' for habitual routines and 'event' for scheduled recurring occurrences; resolve relative time from the message timestamp.
During CRUD, if a matching memory for the same activity already exists, UPDATE or MERGE it rather than adding a duplicate.

nearby_not_selected.name: Extract Family Pet Ownership
nearby_not_selected.description: When a speaker references a pet as belonging to their family or household (including via a photo), during extraction.
content: During extraction, if a message links a pet to the speaker's own family or household (e.g., 'my family's dog', 'our dog', a photo described as my family's pet), create a memory that the speaker had that pet.
Do not require an explicit statement like 'I grew up with a dog'; owning a family pet in the past implies it was part of the speaker's upbringing.
Skip pet mentions that clearly belong to someone else (e.g., a friend's dog) or that are generic with no owner.
Record the speaker as subject and use event or relationship memory kinds as appropriate; stop after extracting the ownership fact—do not expand into extra searches or unrelated pet details.
